WhatsApp Could Expand Agent Reach

Together, the projects build on CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s push to create AI-driven businesses beyond Meta’s core advertising operation.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) reclaimed its top spot as the best-performing asset over the past decade, narrowly edging out Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Bitcoin Edged Past Nvidia in 10-Year Gains

Mark Harvey, a widely followed Bitcoin investor and analyst, shared a table of major assets and their 10-year returns.

Bitcoin claimed the top spot with a staggering 13,491% return, while Nvidia, a key gauge of AI enthusiasm and the wider U.S. stock market, finished a close second at 13,428%.

Nvidia Has Had the Better Off Bitcoin Lately

It’s worth noting that over a shorter timeframe, Nvidia has clearly outperformed Bitcoin.

Both Nvidia and Bitcoin are risk-laden investments, and traders must navigate their inherent volatility to profit. For that, analysts track the Sharpe Ratio, a measure of risk-adjusted returns. 

Bitcoin’s Sharpe Ratio stood at 7 as of this writing, according to TradingView, indicating that investment in the stock was generating positive returns above the risk-free rate. In Nvidia’s case, the ratio was -1.20, suggesting that the expected return was lower than that of a risk-free investment.

Among the remaining “Mag 7” names, Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) delivered gains of 740% and 591%, respectively, in the last 10 years.

Compared to Bitcoin, gold underperformed, gaining just 248% in the last decade.

Rasgon Sees Rubin Driving Data Center Growth

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC on Saturday that he expects NVIDIA to report strong quarterly results. However, he will closely watch management’s comments on the Rubin ramp.

NVIDIA’s three-year outlook points to roughly $500 billion in data center revenue next year, Rasgon said. Still, Rubin build plans suggest revenue could exceed that level. Therefore, he wants to know whether management will raise its expectations.

Margins And AI Financing Draw Attention

Rasgon will also watch whether NVIDIA can keep gross margins in the mid-70% range as memory and wafer prices rise. Management previously indicated that margins could remain near current levels.

In addition, he wants more details about NVIDIA’s financial support for major data center projects. Rasgon sees the company’s balance sheet as a strategic advantage.

Using excess cash to support customers could expand the AI ecosystem, he said. It could also strengthen long-term demand for NVIDIA’s products.

Rubin Could Extend NVIDIA’s Stock Momentum

Rasgon cautioned that strong earnings may not produce an immediate stock gain. Other semiconductor companies have recently reported solid results without receiving a positive market reaction.

However, he believes NVIDIA remains essential to the global AI infrastructure buildout. The stock trailed several semiconductor peers for much of the past year but has recently started to outperform the group.

Rasgon sees the Rubin cycle as a potential catalyst for further gains. Historically, NVIDIA’s new product cycles have created favorable conditions for the stock.

World Trade Securities CEO Nicholas Mugalli has publicly called out Citadel Securities, claiming Ken Griffin’s firm is “short bonds” and complaining about Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s expanded buyback operations because the official yield caps are “crushing their squeeze”—Citadel Securities characterized the intervention as ‘financial repression’ at the margin.

Behind Citadel’s ‘Financial Repression’ Critique

In a recent macro note, Citadel Securities strategist Nohshad Shah criticized the Treasury’s decision to double its 10- to 30-year bond buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation.

Shah described the intervention as “financial repression at the margin,” arguing that policymakers are trying to suppress market signals rather than fix underlying fiscal problems caused by procyclical easing.

However, Mugalli countered on X that Citadel Securities’ sudden alarms over inflation hide a self-serving market position. “And by the way, Citadel is short bonds, so when Bessent uses the TGA to cap yields with buybacks, they scream ‘financial repression,'” Mugalli posted. He further added that “crying about inflation now is just Citadel trying to talk the bond market down so they can cover.”

Read Also: Stanley Druckenmiller Slams Scott Bessent’s $4 Billion Treasury Buybacks: ‘This Wasn’t Liquidity Management, It Was Price Management’

Squeezing the Shorts and the Old Quantum Playbook

Mugalli suggested that instead of complaining, legendary macro traders would historically exploit such Treasury maneuvers. Reflecting on past heavyweights, he noted: “I wonder what Bessent, Soros, and Druckenmiller would do if they were still at Quantum Fund… They’d smell blood in the water and squeeze the Treasury until the yield curve broke completely.”

While Mugalli agrees with Stanley Druckenmiller‘s recent high-profile op-ed calling for the government to “let the bond market speak”, he asserts that current Wall Street outrage over the Treasury’s actions is largely driven by massive short-sellers who are unexpectedly caught on the losing side of official liquidity support.

At the last check, the 30-year Treasury bond yielded 5.23%, the 10-year Treasury bond was at 4.70%, and the two-year bond was at 4.24%.

It was lower by 6.03% year-to-date, down 0.83% over the last month and 5.16% over the last year.

An ‘Economic D-Day’ or a Dud?

In his recent Substack newsletter, Paul Krugman dissected Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s proposed “economic D-Day” against Iran. While the administration claims Iran is already defeated and desperate for a deal, Krugman points out fundamental flaws in their strategy.

He warns that this economic pressure campaign will “fail as thoroughly as the military campaign.” Due to the “sheer scale of the U.S. military failure in the Persian Gulf,” which includes abandoned U.S. bases and a strained Navy, maintaining an effective blockade on Iranian exports has become increasingly difficult.

Threats Built on Exhausted Credibility

The Treasury Department recently announced expanded sanctions targeting individuals and vessels, threatening to cut off countries trading with Iran from the dollar-based financial system. However, its initial list notably omitted Chinese financial institutions.

Krugman dismissed Bessent’s grandiose claims of globally isolating Iran, arguing the administration’s credibility is already “exhausted” from constantly backtracking and indiscriminately imposing tariffs.

He predicts that those who “really have the goods – China, in this case – smell the scent of desperation.”

Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group, told Benzinga that Nvidia is the "cleanest test" of whether AI infrastructure demand has actually peaked.

Newman expects revenue could reach $94 billion to $95 billion, potentially exceeding Nvidia’s guidance, with October-quarter revenue potentially climbing toward $107 billion to $108 billion and eventually topping $110 billion.

If Nvidia continues delivering accelerating revenue while keeping gross margins in the mid-70% range, Newman said it would be difficult to argue that the underlying compute cycle is already rolling over.

Nvidia Hyperscaler Growth Faces Its Next Big Test

Beyond the headline revenue number, Newman said, "The biggest thing I am watching beyond the headline beat is the Hyperscale versus ACIE split."

He said Nvidia’s decision to break out Data Center demand between major cloud and internet companies and its broader AI Cloud, Industrial and Enterprise customer base gives investors a clearer view of whether AI demand is expanding beyond the industry’s biggest buyers.

Hyperscalers such as Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) have driven much of the AI infrastructure boom.

U.S. hyperscalers are expected to spend roughly $916 billion on capital expenditures over the next 12 months, with consensus estimates projecting that figure to rise to nearly $1.2 trillion the year after.

Newman believes the next phase could become more durable if ACIE growth accelerates rapidly, signaling that enterprises, industrial companies, sovereign customers and neoclouds are taking on more AI compute demand.

Strong Nvidia Earnings May Not Mean Higher NVDA Stock

Still, Newman cautioned that an earnings beat alone may not send Nvidia shares higher.

With expectations already elevated, investors could punish the stock if Nvidia’s results or forward guidance fail to exceed what has already been priced in.

"I have very little confidence in predicting whether the stock will be up or down the next morning," Newman said, while maintaining that Nvidia’s longer-term earnings trajectory remains the more important factor.

Nvidia shares have declined following five of the company’s past six earnings reports, with the last earnings-related move of 10% or more occurring in February 2024

Newman sees a potential path toward more than $15 in calendar 2027 EPS and roughly $20 in 2028, meaning continued earnings growth could drive Nvidia shares without requiring another major expansion in its valuation.

Nvidia Earnings Estimates Put AI Demand In Focus

In May, Nvidia reported first-quarter revenue of $81.615 billion, an 85% increase year over year, topping Wall Street’s $78.796 billion estimate.

The company guided for second-quarter revenue of $89.18 billion to $92.82 billion, above the Street’s $86.62 billion forecast at the time.

For the latest quarter, Wall Street expects Nvidia to report $2.07 in adjusted EPS on $91.91 billion in revenue, up from $1.04 in adjusted EPS and $46.74 billion in revenue a year earlier.

The estimates put the spotlight on whether AI demand remains strong enough to support Nvidia’s lofty growth expectations.

According to Benzinga Pro data, options markets are pricing in a 5.35% move for Nvidia shares following the earnings report.

While that is the smallest implied move among the companies on the list, the stakes remain significant: Nvidia has a market capitalization of about $5.26 trillion, implying roughly $282 billion in market value could be at stake.

Oil dropped to a one-week low Tuesday after Washington unveiling its most sweeping sanctions campaign against Iran on record.

West Texas Intermediate traded near $82.35 a barrel by 7:38 a.m. ET, down 3.2% below Monday’s settlement around $84.89. Brent crude for October fell 2.92% to $89.48.

The market it is pricing the odds that the war restarts, and every headline since Monday afternoon has pushed those odds lower.

Chart: WTI crude, hourly. Source: TradingView

The Headline That Actually Moved Crude

Two reports landed overnight.

The New York Times, citing an internal State Department document, reported that Washington is preparing to send Foreign Service officers back to Middle East embassies evacuated during the war, with returns possible as early as this week across eight host countries including Kuwait, Iraq, Qatar and Israel.

Then Al Arabiya reported that Pakistan Army Chief Asim Munir had carried a U.S. proposal to Tehran offering to halt the naval blockade and lift sanctions in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending attacks by Iran-aligned groups.

Iranian officials said they would respond after domestic consultations.

Neither headline promises a deal.

Both tell traders the same thing: nobody in Washington is preparing for the next strike.

Why The Sanctions Package Was Read As Dovish

Monday’s announcement set the tone.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the package Monday, calling it an economic D-Day and sanctioning about 60 entities, individuals and vessels across shipping, gold, aviation, technology and digital assets.

But the enforcement was deferred.

What Bessent did not do was name which of Iran’s trading partners face secondary penalties, or say when.

Asked why, he said: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”

Saxo Bank commodity strategy head Ole Hansen said the pivot from military escalation to economic pressure has drained some of the market’s supply anxiety, noting the package landed softer than traders had feared.

“Traders increasingly focused on signs that the immediate risk of another major escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict may be receding,” he said on Tuesday.

What Cheaper Crude Does To Everything Else

Falling oil pulled Treasury yields down with it. The 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.662% from 4.704%.

Lower energy costs feed straight into lower expected inflation, which loosens the constraint on the Federal Reserve.

Equities took the handoff.

SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) rose 0.48% in premarket trading. Industrial Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLI) gained 0.92% and Delta Air Lines Inc. (NYSE:DAL) climbed 2.12%

Energy went the other way.

United States Oil Fund LP (NYSE:USO) fell 3.57% premarket, Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLE) dropped 1.00% and Occidental Petroleum Corp. (NYSE:OXY) lost 1.75%.

He explicitly criticized the effort to influence the slope of the yield curve. “I call this the ‘Bessent twist,’ and I do not think it is a good idea,” Siegel wrote. The core issue, according to Siegel, is a looming policy clash.

While newly appointed Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh emphasizes allowing markets to send authentic economic signals, the Treasury appears interested in deliberately altering those very signals.

Siegel cautioned that long-term rates reflect vital expectations for inflation, economic growth, deficits, and risk premiums. He warned that attempting to manage this market could ultimately “damage credibility” if the intervention fails.

A Normal Market and Muddled Signals

Yardeni argues that a 10-year bond yield between 4% and 5% is simply “back to normal” and a “sign of a healthy economy” that can handle current borrowing levels from both the government and technology hyperscalers.

However, Yardeni notes that the Treasury’s deployment of its extensive toolkit to suppress yields creates a severe headache for monetary policymakers. “It’s going to muck up things for Kevin Warsh because Kevin Warsh is looking for signals from the bond market,” Yardeni explained.

“And here the Treasury is using its toolkit to send a different message.” Ultimately, analysts fear this intervention creates a critical blind spot for the Federal Reserve right as it attempts to navigate its inflation outlook and clarify its reaction function for the market.

Suppressing rates, he argues, sugarcoats interest-cost projections and allows politicians to delay necessary entitlement reforms.

Paying the Market’s Invoice

Rather than managing yields, Druckenmiller insists the Treasury should return buybacks to small, scheduled liquidity operations and focus on addressing the primary deficit.

OpenAI has terminated a number of ChatGPT accounts from Russia, accusing them of participating in a clandestine online misinformation operation.

The Sam Altman-led company discovered the issue while analyzing AI-generated social media posts, leading to the identification of a broader influence operation, according to an OpenAI blog post on Tuesday.

The operation was primarily based around a website that hosted plagiarized and wrongly attributed academic work, a ‘sovereignty’ index favoring Vladimir Putin‘s Russia, and attempts to hide the operators’ Russian roots, as per OpenAI. The operators leveraged Russian prompts to generate social media comments posted on platforms such as Substack, Telegram, Meta Platform Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:META) Facebook, and LinkedIn. They also directed ChatGPT to mask any linguistic indications of their Russian origin.

The majority of the generated content promoted an organization called the International Burke Institute (IBI). The IBI’s website features articles copied from legitimate academic sources, sometimes falsely attributed. The influence operation also created a ‘sovereignty index’ that lauded Russia and criticized Western nations.

While the immediate impact of the operation appears to be limited, OpenAI stressed that the operation’s significance lies in the infrastructure it had established. The AI-generated posts pointed to a seemingly credible institution, complete with alleged experts, republished academic work, and a purported proprietary risk index.

OpenAI Flags Rising AI Influence Risks

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) reports earnings Wednesday in what may be the clearest test yet of whether Big Tech’s enormous AI infrastructure buildout is still accelerating. The largest technology companies are set to spend more than $700 billion on capex this year.

But Steve Neamtz, CEO of Yorkville America, says some of the most important constraints are emerging beyond the chips themselves.

“The $700 billion number is real, and it matters, but I think the more interesting question is where that money actually has to go,” Neamtz told Benzinga.

AI Spending Hits Physical Constraints

Neamtz points to three bottlenecks further down the supply chain. The most immediate is memory, storage and the power needed to run it all. “Compute has scaled faster than that layer can keep up,” he said.

That concern already looks timely. Some of Nvidia’s customers have reportedly been told that prices for some AI servers will rise more than 15%, largely because of soaring memory costs.

The second is critical minerals. By 2030, AI data centers could require the equivalent of about 3% of today’s global rare-earth demand, according to estimates cited by Sprott.

The third is labor. The construction industry needs an estimated 349,000 additional U.S. workers in 2026, according to Associated Builders and Contractors, a figure covering the whole industry rather than data centers alone.

“It really isn’t a capital problem — it’s a physical one,” Neamtz said.

The scale of the spending isn’t what worries investors, in his view. What matters is whether management can point to a genuine constraint and explain what the capex unlocks. Spending that looks reactive is more likely to be treated as a drain on cash.

“It’s less about the size of the number and more about whether there’s a coherent story behind it,” he said.

Nvidia Gives Investors the Next Read

Wall Street expects Nvidia to report revenue of about $92.2 billion Wednesday, nearly double last year’s figure, and Reuters describes the results as a test of the AI spending boom’s sustainability.

Prediction market traders expect the physical buildout to keep growing. Kalshi traders currently see a 66% chance the U.S. ends 2026 with at least 5,300 data centers, a 52% chance of at least 5,400 and a 46% chance of reaching 5,500. That compares with 4,313 U.S. data centers as of June 1, 2026, according to Kalshi.

Neamtz will be listening for signs that demand is still running ahead of supply across the AI infrastructure chain. He’ll watch whether companies describe lead times and capacity shortages as easing or tightening.

“If it’s still tightening, that tells you the buildout hasn’t hit its ceiling yet,” he said.

If supply begins catching up with demand, Neamtz sees the investment opportunity entering a different phase.

“The opportunity shifts from infrastructure scarcity to whoever can actually put that capacity to work most efficiently,” he said.

Gene Munster on Nvidia Earnings

"I expect them to do what they have done over the past few quarters: beat by 4% and raise revenue guidance for October by 3%," Munster wrote in a blog post.

Munster said investors will want to see hyperscaler growth of 8% year-over-year and ACIE (data centers) growth of 150% year-over-year. The investor says it’s important that ACIE has higher growth, as that is the segment that has "more potential to drive long-term growth."

"The Data Center segment split that began to be reported last quarter underscores that Nvidia’s business is becoming less dependent on hyperscalers. This is a positive for the story."

SpaceX represented around 4% of revenue in the quarter and has the potential to become a 10% customer by the end of calendar 2027, Munster said.

For Nvidia, the company has four horsemen, according to Munster: Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. Those four make up around 80% of Nvidia’s data center revenue. Munster says SpaceX is becoming the “fifth horseman.”

On the subject of China, Munster doesn’t expect any new "material commentary" on the potential revenue from the country.

"China is such a massive opportunity, about a quarter of global GPU spending, that the topic of when Nvidia can get back in there is almost guaranteed to come up on the call."

Wall Street’s next commodity may not sit in a barrel or a warehouse. It may be an hour of computing time on a chip from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Kalshi’s GPU rental markets generated $4.4 million in notional volume through July 27, according to data analytics firm Allium. That is tiny compared with oil or gold markets, but meaningful for a product that barely existed weeks earlier.

The real test is whether these early markets can establish a reliable forward price for AI computing power.

$4.4 Million Is Small, but Not Nothing

Bloomberg Opinion argued Monday that “barely anyone” is trading compute contracts, noting Kalshi’s most popular August market has generated just over $100,000.

Bloomberg measured a single contract, while Allium’s total covers Kalshi markets across five Nvidia chips. Kalshi’s total was roughly 15 times the $285,000 traded on rival Polymarket.

That is nowhere near enough volume for a large company to hedge its computing costs. But for such a new market, it shows that traders are interested in GPU prices.

Is Kalshi Producing a Useful Price?

Allium examined six completed weekly markets tracking Nvidia B200 rental prices. Two days before settlement, Kalshi’s forecasts were a median 10% away from the final price while remaining within 2.2% of the current spot price. That suggests traders were largely following spot prices rather than anticipating where they would move next.

That is not a compelling forecasting record, but neither is it disastrous for a market that had existed for only weeks. Six contracts is far too small a sample for a firm verdict, particularly while traders are still learning how to price compute. What to watch is whether Kalshi’s forecasts begin moving ahead of spot prices as participation grows.

Why Wall Street Is Watching

CME Group Inc. (NASDAQ:CME) plans to launch futures tracking monthly rental costs for Nvidia’s H100 and B200 chips on Oct. 5, pending regulatory review. The exchange compares compute’s development with oil’s evolution from spot trading into a global derivatives market.

Unlike barrels of crude, GPU hours are not interchangeable. Their price depends on the chip, location, network performance and reliability. But a futures market does not require every unit to be identical. It only needs a benchmark that moves closely enough with customers’ costs to provide a useful hedge.

Kalshi’s early volume shows there is interest in trading compute prices, even if the market is not ready for large corporate hedges.

Recent flow data show heavy allocations to mega-cap equity vehicles such as State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), while cash-like Treasury ETFs including iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (NYSE:SGOV) and iShares 1-3 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:SHY) keep absorbing demand from investors seeking yield without long-duration pain.

This barbell approach, popularized by Nassim Nicholas Taleb, is maximizing exposure at opposite ends of the risk spectrum while minimizing the middle. However, when such an extreme approach becomes popular, it creates a structural gap.

If capital crowds into high-beta tech and short-term fixed income, moderate-risk core gets left behind.

Abandoned Mid-Caps and Cyclicals

The divergence is no longer subtle. Data from LSEG Liper, as reported by Reuters, show that in the last week, large-cap U.S. equity funds took in about $9.58 billion. Mid-cap and small-cap funds lost roughly $809 million and $70 million, respectively.

The pattern shows cannibalization. The barbell isn’t adding risk at one end and safety at the other; rather, it’s draining breadth from the middle. Over the last 12 months, equal-weight and value-tilted exposure lagged as investors pursued AI optionality and earnings visibility even at a premium.

Crowded AI Meets Rising Macro Friction

The first pressure point is earnings concentration risk—especially around Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), which has become a guidepost for the AI spend cycle.

Ahead of tomorrow’s earnings, Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group, called the company the "cleanest test" of whether infrastructure demand has peaked.

"The biggest thing I am watching beyond the headline beat is the Hyperscale versus ACIE (AI Cloud, Industrial and Enterprise) split," he said.

In a market priced for persistent upside, even a modest deceleration in revenue momentum or margin trajectory could force investors to de-risk the growth end of the barbell.

The second pressure point is the defensive leg itself. Short-duration Treasuries have worked as a high-liquidity shelter, but reinvestment risk rises as front-end dynamics shift and longer yields stay volatile.

Commenting on the Treasury’s bond intervention, Kelsey Berro of JPMorgan Asset Management warned that lower yields "can’t be sustained unless it’s supported by the fundamentals."

Meanwhile, Mohamed El-Erian sees the broad macro picture as "a race going on between the promise and the earnings that comes with AI and the cost of funding all that."

A Looming Snapback

If either side of the barbell weakens, capital has to go somewhere. The most likely destination is the market segment starved of flows: mid-caps, cyclicals and traditional value. That is the overlooked asymmetry in today’s consensus trade.

By concentrating risk and safety at opposite poles, investors have engineered what can fairly be called a "hollow middle." If expectations crack at the top or the carry thesis softens at the bottom, the unwind could be abrupt.

It could be less of a gentle rebalancing than a forceful decompression into the assets largely overlooked in this quarter.

The watchlist for such a scenario includes ETFs with broad-market concentration like Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), iShares Core S&P Mid-Cap ETF (NYSE:IJH),  and hard cyclicals like the Industrial Select Sector SPDR (NYSE:XLI).
